title: The Constitutional Development of India
gist: Follow the transfer of power: Company trade, Crown rule, then independence.

points.html: 1773: the Regulating Act created the office of Governor-General of Bengal and provided for the Supreme Court at Calcutta; the Court opened in 1774.
1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except tea and trade with China; 1833 ended its commercial role and made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.
1853 separated legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council. The 1858 Act transferred rule from the Company to the Crown.
1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims; 1919 introduced provincial dyarchy; 1935 provided provincial autonomy and an all-India federation that never came into operation.

confusion: Keep enactment and operation separate. The Federal Court began in 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935; a federation proposed by that Act was never established.
recall: Which Act made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India?
The Charter Act, 1833. William Bentinck became the first holder of the new office.
How did 1919 and 1935 differ at the provincial level?
1919 divided provincial subjects under dyarchy. 1935 replaced that arrangement with provincial autonomy.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Keep enactment and operation separate. The Federal Court began in 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935; a federation proposed by that Act was never established.

title: Constituent Assembly and Making of the Constitution
gist: Separate the Assembly's composition, its office-holders, and the Constitution's dates.

points.html: The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 provided for a 389-member Constituent Assembly: 296 from British India and 93 from princely states; membership became 299 after partition.
The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary chairman; Rajendra Prasad became its President on 11 December.
B.N. Rau was constitutional adviser. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which was appointed on 29 August 1947.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949. Members signed on 24 January 1950; the main commencement date was 26 January 1950.

confusion: The Constituent Assembly was indirectly elected through provincial legislatures; it was not directly elected by universal adult suffrage.
recall: Who was constitutional adviser, and who chaired the Drafting Committee?
B.N. Rau was adviser; B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee. These were different roles.
Why are 26 November and 26 January both important?
26 November 1949 marks adoption; 26 January 1950 marks general commencement. Some provisions operated from the adoption date.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The Constituent Assembly was indirectly elected through provincial legislatures; it was not directly elected by universal adult suffrage.
memory_hook: Meet - adopt - sign - commence: December 1946; November 1949; January 1950; January 1950.

title: Important Committees of Constituent Assembly
gist: Learn committees by the job they performed, then attach their chairperson.

points.html: Jawaharlal Nehru chaired the Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees; Sardar Patel chaired the Provincial Constitution and Advisory Committees.
Rajendra Prasad chaired the Rules of Procedure and Steering Committees, as well as the ad hoc National Flag Committee.

Ambedkar chaired the seven-member Drafting Committee: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Mohammad Saadullah, B.L. Mitter and D.P. Khaitan were the other original members.
N. Madhav Rau replaced B.L. Mitter; T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan. Keep original and replacement members separate.

confusion: Nehru and Patel were major Assembly leaders, but neither was a member of the Drafting Committee.
recall: Which two major committees did Nehru chair?
Union Powers and Union Constitution. The shared word Union is a useful learning hook.
Who replaced Mitter and Khaitan?
N. Madhav Rau replaced B.L. Mitter; T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Nehru and Patel were major Assembly leaders, but neither was a member of the Drafting Committee.

title: Sources of the Constitution
gist: The Constitution adapted ideas to Indian needs; a source-country question tests the specific feature.

points.html: Britain: parliamentary government, cabinet system, rule of law, legislative procedure and parliamentary privileges.
USA: fundamental rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, the Vice-President and impeachment of the President.
Ireland: Directive Principles, the presidential election method and nomination to the Rajya Sabha. Canada: a strong Centre and residuary powers.
Australia: Concurrent List and joint sitting; South Africa: amendment procedure and Rajya Sabha elections; USSR: fundamental duties; Japan: procedure established by law.

confusion: Do not confuse nomination to the Rajya Sabha, associated with Ireland, with election of its members, associated with South Africa.
recall: Which source is associated with Directive Principles?
Ireland. Fundamental Rights are associated with the USA, so the two should be learned as a pair.
Which country's model is linked to the Concurrent List?
Australia. The book also associates joint sitting with Australia.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Do not confuse nomination to the Rajya Sabha, associated with Ireland, with election of its members, associated with South Africa.

title: Parts of Indian Constitution
gist: A Part is a large subject folder; an Article is an individual provision inside it.

points.html: The original Constitution had 22 Parts. Later additions include IV-A (duties), IX-A (municipalities), IX-B (cooperatives), and XIV-A (tribunals); Part VII was omitted.
Parts III, IV and IV-A respectively cover Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.
Part V concerns the Union; Part VI concerns the states; Part XI concerns Union-state relations; Part XII concerns finance, property, contracts and suits.
Part XV covers elections; XVI special provisions for certain classes; XVII official language; XVIII emergencies; XX constitutional amendment.

confusion: The suffix matters: Part IX is Panchayats; Part IX-A is Municipalities. An inserted Part does not renumber all later Parts.
recall: Match Parts III, IV and IV-A to their subjects.
III: Fundamental Rights; IV: Directive Principles; IV-A: Fundamental Duties.
Where do you find amendment procedure?
Part XX, principally Article 368. Elections belong to Part XV.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The suffix matters: Part IX is Panchayats; Part IX-A is Municipalities. An inserted Part does not renumber all later Parts.
memory_hook: III rights, IV goals, IV-A duties.

title: Articles of the Constitution
gist: Build Article clusters before learning isolated numbers.

points.html: Articles 14-18 concern equality; 19-22 freedom and personal protections; 23-24 exploitation; 25-28 religion; 29-30 cultural and educational protections; 32 constitutional remedies.
Article 54 concerns presidential election; 61 impeachment; 72 pardons; 74 ministerial advice; 76 the Attorney General; 123 presidential ordinances; 148 the CAG.
Article 124 concerns the Supreme Court; 143 advisory jurisdiction; 214 High Courts; 226 High Court writs; 280 the Finance Commission; 324 the Election Commission.
Article 300A protects property; 343 concerns the Union's official language; 352 national emergency; 356 President's Rule; 360 financial emergency; 368 amendment.

confusion: Article 300A concerns property. It must not be confused with Article 330A, which concerns women's representation in the Lok Sabha.
recall: Which Article creates the Finance Commission?
Article 280. Article 324 concerns the Election Commission; the bodies have different constitutional jobs.
Which writ jurisdiction is wider, Article 32 or 226?
Article 226: High Courts may enforce Fundamental Rights and other legal rights. Article 32 is for Fundamental Rights.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Article 300A concerns property. It must not be confused with Article 330A, which concerns women's representation in the Lok Sabha.

title: Schedules
gist: Use the Schedules as twelve attachments to the constitutional text.

points.html: Schedules 1-4: states/UTs; specified office-holders' emoluments; oaths; allocation of Rajya Sabha seats.
Schedules 5 and 6: Scheduled Areas/Scheduled Tribes administration and autonomous tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram respectively.
Schedule 7 divides legislative subjects into Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Schedule 8 lists languages; Schedule 9 concerns specified laws and their constitutional protection.
Schedule 10 concerns defection; 11 lists 29 Panchayat subjects; 12 lists 18 municipal subjects. The original Constitution had eight Schedules.

comparison: Scheduled Areas / specified north-eastern tribal areas
confusion: A law in the Ninth Schedule is not automatically beyond all judicial review. Learn the basic-structure qualification with the source explanation.
recall: Which Schedule contains the three legislative lists?
The Seventh Schedule. The Eighth is about languages, not legislative powers.
How do the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules differ?
The Eleventh has 29 Panchayat subjects; the Twelfth has 18 municipal subjects.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A law in the Ninth Schedule is not automatically beyond all judicial review. Learn the basic-structure qualification with the source explanation.
memory_hook: The last three: defection, village, town - 10, 11, 12.

title: The Preamble
gist: Read the Preamble as the Constitution's statement of identity, purposes and authority.

points.html: The Objectives Resolution was moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947; it informed the Preamble.
The Preamble describes India as sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and a republic. Its authority comes from the people.
Its goals include social, economic and political justice; liberty; equality; and fraternity assuring individual dignity and national unity and integrity.
The 42nd Amendment, 1976 added Socialist, Secular and Integrity. The Preamble is part of the Constitution and aids interpretation; it is not independently enforceable.

confusion: Republic means an elected head of state rather than hereditary succession. Democratic and republic describe different features.
recall: Which three words were added in 1976?
Socialist, Secular and Integrity, through the 42nd Amendment.
Can the Preamble by itself provide an enforceable legal remedy?
No. It guides interpretation and expresses constitutional purposes; enforceable rights are found in operative provisions.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Republic means an elected head of state rather than hereditary succession. Democratic and republic describe different features.

title: The Governance System
gist: Ask three different questions: who rules, how the executive stays in office, and how power is divided.

points.html: In parliamentary government the executive is politically responsible to the legislature. In a presidential system the executive has a separately fixed constitutional position.
India combines a parliamentary system with a federal distribution of powers and a strong Union. A parliamentary system does not itself mean a unitary state.
The President is the constitutional head of the Union; the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister exercises government through the constitutional system of advice and responsibility.
The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary decides disputes and reviews legality. Constitutional checks prevent concentration of power.

comparison: How the head of state holds office
confusion: Separation of powers in India is not a complete personnel separation: ministers are normally members of the legislature.
recall: What is the core test of a parliamentary executive?
Political responsibility to the legislature, especially the elected lower house.
Can a country be both federal and parliamentary?
Yes. These describe different dimensions: territorial power division and executive responsibility.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Separation of powers in India is not a complete personnel separation: ministers are normally members of the legislature.

title: National Symbols
gist: Learn each national symbol with its adoption date and the detail that distinguishes it.

points.html: The national flag was adopted on 22 July 1947. Its length-to-height ratio is 3:2; the navy-blue Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes.
The State Emblem is adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath; it was adopted on 26 January 1950. Satyameva Jayate comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.
Jana Gana Mana is the national anthem, composed by Rabindranath Tagore. Vande Mataram, by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, is the national song.
The standard full version of the anthem takes about 52 seconds. The national calendar uses the Saka era.

confusion: The flag was adopted before independence; the State Emblem was adopted when India became a republic.
recall: What are the flag's ratio and wheel-spoke count?
Length to height is 3:2; the Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes.
Which text supplies Satyameva Jayate?
The Mundaka Upanishad. It is the motto beneath the State Emblem.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The flag was adopted before independence; the State Emblem was adopted when India became a republic.

title: States and Union Territories
gist: Distinguish a state's creation, its name change and a change in constitutional status.

points.html: Article 1 describes India as a Union of States. Article 2 concerns admission or establishment of new states; Article 3 concerns formation and alteration of existing states.
A state-reorganisation bill under Article 3 needs the President's recommendation. The affected state legislature gives its views; its consent is not a constitutional veto.
The States Reorganisation Act and Seventh Amendment, 1956 reshaped state organisation. Andhra State had already been formed in 1953.
The book's territorial snapshot is 28 states and 8 Union Territories. Keep older PYQs about pre-reorganisation India in their original time context.

confusion: The first state created on a linguistic basis after independence was Andhra State in 1953; do not substitute the later name Andhra Pradesh without checking the question's date.
recall: Can the affected state veto an Article 3 reorganisation?
No. Its legislature's views are sought, but Parliament is not bound by those views.
Why must state-count questions carry a date?
Reorganisation changes totals and representation. A historical answer can differ from the book's later snapshot.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The first state created on a linguistic basis after independence was Andhra State in 1953; do not substitute the later name Andhra Pradesh without checking the question's date.

title: The Citizenship
gist: The Constitution sets the starting framework; citizenship legislation supplies continuing rules.

points.html: Articles 5-11 concern citizenship. Article 11 enables Parliament to regulate acquisition and termination by law.
The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides routes including birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory; conditions differ between routes and over time.
India has single citizenship. An OCI card is not Indian citizenship and does not confer the political rights of an Indian citizen.
Loss of citizenship is discussed as renunciation, termination and deprivation. Treat the CAA, 2019 and its rules as statutory provisions with specific conditions, not a general citizenship grant.

comparison: Place of birth / parentage, subject to law
confusion: Living in India, having Indian ancestry and holding an OCI card do not by themselves mean that someone is an Indian citizen.
recall: Which Article gives Parliament power to regulate citizenship?
Article 11. The detailed continuing rules are in legislation such as the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Does OCI mean dual Indian citizenship?
No. OCI is a statutory cardholder status, not a second Indian citizenship.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Living in India, having Indian ancestry and holding an OCI card do not by themselves mean that someone is an Indian citizen.

title: Fundamental Rights
gist: For every right, connect its holder, its protection and the court remedy.

points.html: Part III covers Articles 12-35. Article 14 protects equality before law; Articles 15 and 16 address discrimination and public employment; 17 abolishes untouchability; 18 addresses titles.
Article 19 protects specified freedoms of citizens, subject to constitutional restrictions. Articles 20 and 21 protect persons; Article 21A concerns education for ages 6-14.
Articles 23-24 concern exploitation, 25-28 religion, and 29-30 cultural and educational protections. Article 29 is not confined to minority communities.

Article 32 provides Supreme Court remedies for Fundamental Rights; Article 226 allows High Courts to protect Fundamental Rights and other legal rights. Property is protected under Article 300A outside Part III.

comparison: Require performance of a public duty
Prevent excess jurisdiction / quash an invalid order
Question authority to hold public office
confusion: Rights are not suspended identically in every emergency. Articles 358 and 359 have different triggers and effects; Articles 20 and 21 are protected from Article 359 orders.
recall: Why is High Court writ jurisdiction wider than Article 32?
Article 226 covers other legal rights as well as Fundamental Rights; Article 32 is tied to Fundamental Rights.
Which writ tests unlawful detention?
Habeas corpus. It may reach detention by a public authority or a private person.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Rights are not suspended identically in every emergency. Articles 358 and 359 have different triggers and effects; Articles 20 and 21 are protected from Article 359 orders.
memory_hook: Body - duty - stop - quash - office: the five writ problems.

title: Directive Principles of State Policy
gist: Directive Principles describe the kind of society government should work towards.

points.html: Part IV, Articles 36-51, contains Directive Principles. Article 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
Article 39 concerns distributive and social aims; 39A equal justice and free legal aid; 40 village panchayats; 41 work, education and public assistance within the state's capacity.
Article 44 concerns a uniform civil code; 45 early childhood care and education below age six; 48A environment; 50 separation of judiciary from executive; 51 international peace.
Rights and Directive Principles are meant to work together. Court decisions and amendments shape their relationship; neither is a licence to ignore the rest of the Constitution.

confusion: Non-justiciable does not mean optional in constitutional purpose. It means a court cannot enforce a Directive Principle in the same manner as a Fundamental Right.
recall: Which Article explains the legal status of Directive Principles?
Article 37: they are not enforceable by courts, yet are fundamental in governance.
How do Articles 21A and 45 divide education by age?
21A concerns free compulsory education for ages 6-14; Article 45 concerns early childhood care and education below six.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Non-justiciable does not mean optional in constitutional purpose. It means a court cannot enforce a Directive Principle in the same manner as a Fundamental Right.

title: Fundamental Duties
gist: Duties ask what citizens owe the constitutional community.

points.html: Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A, Article 51A. Ten were inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976; the 86th Amendment, 2002 added the education-related duty.
Duties cover the Constitution and national symbols, freedom-struggle ideals, sovereignty and integrity, defence, harmony, women's dignity and composite culture.
They also concern environment and compassion for living creatures, scientific temper and inquiry, public property and non-violence, and excellence.
The eleventh duty concerns a parent or guardian providing educational opportunities to a child or ward aged 6-14.

confusion: A duty is not automatically an individually enforceable punishment provision. Legislation may give effect to a duty.
recall: Where are Fundamental Duties located?
Part IV-A, Article 51A. The letter A distinguishes it from Article 51 in the Directive Principles.
Which amendment added the eleventh duty?
The 86th Amendment, 2002, concerning educational opportunity for children aged 6-14.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A duty is not automatically an individually enforceable punishment provision. Legislation may give effect to a duty.

title: The President
gist: Organise the President's chapter into election, tenure, powers and constitutional limits.

points.html: The presidential electoral college consists of elected MPs and elected state MLAs, including the specified legislatures of Delhi and Puducherry; nominated members do not participate.
Election uses proportional representation by the single transferable vote and a secret ballot. The President's term is five years; resignation goes to the Vice-President.
Article 61 provides impeachment for violation of the Constitution. Article 72 provides clemency; Article 123 concerns ordinances.
Under Article 74 the President acts on ministerial advice. Advice may be returned once for reconsideration, after which the reconsidered advice is binding.

comparison: Both Houses' members, including nominated MPs
confusion: Do not include nominated MPs, nominated MLAs or Legislative Council members in the President's electoral college.
recall: Who receives the President's resignation?
The Vice-President. The offices receive each other's resignations under separate constitutional provisions.
Can the President repeatedly return the same ministerial advice?
No. Advice may be reconsidered once; the reconsidered advice is binding.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Do not include nominated MPs, nominated MLAs or Legislative Council members in the President's electoral college.

title: The Vice-President
gist: The Vice-President has one constitutional office and a linked parliamentary role.

points.html: Article 63 provides for the Vice-President. The Vice-President is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The electoral college consists of members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members; state legislators do not vote.
The term is five years. Eligibility includes citizenship, age 35 and qualification for election to the Rajya Sabha.
Removal begins with a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all its then members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, with at least 14 days' notice.

comparison: Does not perform Chairman's duties during that period
confusion: Removal of the Vice-President is not the President's impeachment process. The initiating House and majority requirement differ.
recall: Do nominated MPs vote in the Vice-President's election?
Yes. Both elected and nominated members of both Houses participate; state MLAs do not.
Which House initiates removal?
Rajya Sabha, by a majority of all its then members; Lok Sabha must agree.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Removal of the Vice-President is not the President's impeachment process. The initiating House and majority requirement differ.

title: The Council of Ministers
gist: Track appointment, advice and accountability as different steps.

points.html: The President appoints the Prime Minister and appoints other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice. The Council aids and advises the President.
Article 75 makes the Council collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. A no-confidence motion therefore concerns the government as a whole.
A minister who is not a member of either House must become one within six consecutive months to continue in office.
The 91st Amendment caps the Union Council, including the Prime Minister, at 15% of the Lok Sabha's total membership. Cabinet and Council of Ministers are not identical in size.

confusion: The Prime Minister may be a member of either House. The government's collective responsibility is specifically to the Lok Sabha.
recall: To which House is the Council collectively responsible?
Lok Sabha, under Article 75(3). It is not collective responsibility to the Rajya Sabha.
How long may a non-MP remain a minister without joining Parliament?
Six consecutive months. Continued office then requires membership of either House.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The Prime Minister may be a member of either House. The government's collective responsibility is specifically to the Lok Sabha.

title: The Attorney General and the C.A.G.
gist: The Attorney General advises government; the CAG audits public money.

points.html: Article 76 provides for the Attorney General, appointed by the President and qualified to be a Supreme Court judge; the office is held during the President's pleasure.
The Attorney General may participate in Parliament and its committees when entitled under the Constitution, but has no vote by virtue of that office.
Article 148 provides for the CAG, appointed by the President. Statutory tenure is six years or age 65, whichever comes first.
CAG removal follows the manner and grounds applicable to a Supreme Court judge. Audit reports are submitted to the President or Governor and laid before the appropriate legislature.

confusion: The CAG audits and reports; the Public Accounts Committee is a parliamentary committee. They are not the same institution.
recall: Can the Attorney General vote in Parliament because of the office?
No. The right to speak and participate does not itself confer a vote.
How is the CAG's independence protected on removal?
Removal uses the same manner and grounds as a Supreme Court judge, rather than ordinary executive pleasure.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The CAG audits and reports; the Public Accounts Committee is a parliamentary committee. They are not the same institution.

title: Order of Precedence
gist: Order of precedence is a ceremonial ranking, not a chart of everyday governmental command.

points.html: The President is first in the order of precedence, followed by the Vice-President and then the Prime Minister.
Governors rank in relation to their own states; several office-holders have different placements depending on location and official context.
The Chief Justice of India and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha appear at the same principal rank in the source table.
Use the full source table for tied ranks and territorial qualifications; do not turn it into a simple seniority rule for administration.

comparison: Read the wording beside the office
confusion: A higher ceremonial rank does not mean that an office can issue administrative instructions to every office below it.
recall: Who occupies the first three ranks?
President, Vice-President and Prime Minister, in that order.
Why must a Governor's entry be read with its qualification?
The precedence table distinguishes a Governor's position within and outside the Governor's own state.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A higher ceremonial rank does not mean that an office can issue administrative instructions to every office below it.

title: The Parliament (1)
gist: This chapter is the Parliament's composition and the Lok Sabha's representative structure.

points.html: Article 79 defines Parliament as the President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha. The President is part of Parliament but not a member of either House.
Lok Sabha members are directly elected from territorial constituencies. The minimum age for membership is 25.
The Lok Sabha's normal term is five years from its first meeting unless dissolved sooner. Its quorum is one-tenth of total membership.
Older questions may include Anglo-Indian nominations and earlier state-seat allocations. Keep those historical arrangements distinct from the constitutional position after the 104th Amendment.

comparison: Part of Parliament; belongs to neither House
confusion: The former provision for two Anglo-Indian nominees must not be added to present Lok Sabha composition as if it still operates.
recall: What are Parliament's three components?
The President, the Council of States and the House of the People: Article 79.
What are the minimum age and quorum for Lok Sabha?
Age 25; quorum one-tenth of the House's total membership.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The former provision for two Anglo-Indian nominees must not be added to present Lok Sabha composition as if it still operates.

title: The Parliament (2)
gist: Rajya Sabha represents states and has continuity even when Lok Sabha is dissolved.

points.html: Rajya Sabha's constitutional maximum is 250: up to 238 representatives of states and Union Territories, plus 12 members nominated by the President.
The nominated members have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service.
It is a permanent House; members ordinarily serve six years and about one-third retire every second year. Minimum membership age is 30.
Elected state representatives are chosen by elected MLAs through proportional representation by the single transferable vote. States do not all have equal seat allocations.

confusion: Do not confuse maximum constitutional strength, allocated seats and the number of members actually serving on a particular date.
recall: Why is Rajya Sabha called a permanent House?
It is not dissolved; periodic retirement renews part of its membership.
Which fields qualify for presidential nomination?
Literature, science, art and social service.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Do not confuse maximum constitutional strength, allocated seats and the number of members actually serving on a particular date.

title: The Parliament (3)
gist: The type of bill determines the route, the second House's powers and the majority needed.

points.html: An ordinary bill can generally start in either House. A joint sitting under Article 108 can resolve specified deadlocks, with constitutional exceptions.
A Money Bill under Article 110 starts only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; Rajya Sabha may recommend changes and has 14 days to return it.
A constitutional amendment bill must pass each House separately; there is no joint sitting to break a disagreement.
Question Hour seeks ministerial answers; Zero Hour is a parliamentary practice. A no-confidence motion tests the Council of Ministers' support in Lok Sabha.

comparison: Both Houses; joint sitting possible in specified cases
Lok Sabha lead; Rajya Sabha recommendations in 14 days
confusion: Every Money Bill is a financial bill, but every financial bill is not a Money Bill. Use Article 110's defined contents.
recall: Can a joint sitting pass a constitutional amendment bill?
No. Each House must pass it separately with the required majority.
What can Rajya Sabha do with a Money Bill?
Recommend changes within 14 days. Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Every Money Bill is a financial bill, but every financial bill is not a Money Bill. Use Article 110's defined contents.

title: Parliamentary Committees
gist: Committees allow detailed scrutiny that is difficult in a full sitting of Parliament.

points.html: Standing committees continue on a regular basis; ad hoc committees are formed for a particular task and cease after completing it.
The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members: 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha. It scrutinises public accounts with the help of CAG reports.
The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha. The Committee on Public Undertakings has 22: 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha.
Ministers cannot be members of these financial committees. Distinguish the committee's scrutiny from the executive's spending decisions.

confusion: The Estimates Committee is the one among the three major financial committees that has no Rajya Sabha members.
recall: Which financial committee has 30 members?
Estimates Committee, drawn entirely from Lok Sabha.
Which institution supplies audit findings used by PAC?
The CAG. PAC is a legislative scrutiny body, not the auditor itself.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The Estimates Committee is the one among the three major financial committees that has no Rajya Sabha members.
memory_hook: Financial committees: 22, 30, 22; only Estimates is all Lok Sabha.

title: The Parliamentary Act
gist: For each Act, connect the problem it addresses, its year and its enforcement machinery.

points.html: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 addresses disabilities arising from untouchability; the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 addresses specified atrocities and related safeguards.
The Right to Information Act, 2005 creates a statutory information-access framework, subject to exemptions, procedures and appeals.
The Environment (Protection) Act is from 1986; the Protection of Human Rights Act is from 1993; the Disaster Management Act is from 2005.
A printed question may ask the law in force at an earlier date. Repeals, amendments, territorial changes and renamed laws must retain their date context.

confusion: Do not memorise the old RTI exemption for Jammu and Kashmir or the former fixed Information Commissioner tenure as timeless present law.
recall: Which two major Acts in this chapter date from 2005?
The Right to Information Act and the Disaster Management Act; they deal with different subjects.
Why is an Act's year alone insufficient?
An amendment or repeal can change the rule while leaving the original Act's title and year unchanged.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Do not memorise the old RTI exemption for Jammu and Kashmir or the former fixed Information Commissioner tenure as timeless present law.

title: The Supreme Court
gist: Separate the Supreme Court's institutional structure from the kind of case it is hearing.

points.html: Article 124 concerns the Supreme Court's establishment and constitution. Judges retire at 65; removal requires the special parliamentary process for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
Article 131 concerns specified original federal disputes; Articles 132-136 concern appellate routes; Article 143 concerns presidential references for an advisory opinion.
Article 32 supplies remedies for Fundamental Rights; Article 137 permits review of the Court's judgments; Article 141 makes its declared law binding on courts in India.
Judicial review tests legality and constitutionality. The basic-structure doctrine limits Parliament's constitutional-amending power; PIL concerns access and public-interest adjudication.

confusion: A judicial review of legislation and a review of the Court's own judgment under Article 137 are different uses of the word review.
recall: What does Article 143 concern?
The President's reference for the Supreme Court's advisory opinion.
What is the retirement age of a Supreme Court judge?
65. High Court judges retire at 62.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A judicial review of legislation and a review of the Court's own judgment under Article 137 are different uses of the word review.

title: The Governor
gist: The Governor is a state's constitutional head, usually acting on ministerial advice.

points.html: The President appoints the Governor. Eligibility includes Indian citizenship and age 35; the ordinary term is five years, subject to the President's pleasure.
Article 163 concerns the Council of Ministers' advice and constitutionally permitted discretion. Article 164 concerns appointment of the Chief Minister and other ministers.
Article 161 concerns clemency within the state field; Article 213 concerns ordinances; Article 200 concerns assent, return or reservation of state bills.
The Governor appoints the Chief Minister and may report constitutional failure, but President's Rule under Article 356 is proclaimed by the President.

confusion: The Governor's five-year term is not an absolute guarantee of remaining in office for five years: Article 156 also states presidential pleasure.
recall: Who appoints a Governor?
The President. The Governor is not directly elected by the state's voters.
Which Article provides for state ordinances?
Article 213. Presidential ordinances are under Article 123.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The Governor's five-year term is not an absolute guarantee of remaining in office for five years: Article 156 also states presidential pleasure.

title: The State Legislature
gist: A state legislature may have one House or two; their powers and composition differ.

points.html: Article 169 allows Parliament to create or abolish a Legislative Council after the Assembly passes the specified special-majority resolution.
A Council normally has at least 40 members and no more than one-third of the Assembly's strength. Its members ordinarily serve six years; it is not dissolved.
Article 171 provides approximately one-third each from local bodies and MLAs, one-twelfth each from graduates and teachers, with the remainder nominated by the Governor.
The minimum age is 25 for the Assembly and 30 for the Council. The Council has more limited powers than the Assembly, especially over money and government responsibility.

confusion: A Legislative Council does not have the same constitutional powers as Rajya Sabha. State bicameralism cannot be learned by copying every parliamentary rule.
recall: Who finally creates or abolishes a Legislative Council?
Parliament by law, after the state's Assembly passes the resolution required by Article 169.
What are the Assembly and Council minimum ages?
25 and 30 respectively.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A Legislative Council does not have the same constitutional powers as Rajya Sabha. State bicameralism cannot be learned by copying every parliamentary rule.

title: The High Court
gist: The High Court is the constitutional court for its territory and supervises subordinate courts.

points.html: Article 214 provides for High Courts. Article 231 permits a common High Court for two or more states, or for states and Union Territories.
High Court judges are appointed by the President and retire at 62. Article 217 contains the principal appointment and qualification provisions.
Article 226 allows writs for Fundamental Rights and other legal rights; Article 227 concerns superintendence over courts and tribunals within its territory, with the constitutional exception.
A High Court is a court of record under Article 215. Article 235 concerns control over district and subordinate courts.

comparison: Fundamental Rights and other legal rights
confusion: A state need not have an entirely separate High Court: the Constitution permits common High Courts.
recall: Which Article gives High Courts writ power?
Article 226. Article 227 concerns superintendence.
Does every state require its own distinct High Court?
No. Article 231 permits common High Courts.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A state need not have an entirely separate High Court: the Constitution permits common High Courts.

title: The Centre-State Relations
gist: Federal relations divide into legislative power, administration and finance.

points.html: The Seventh Schedule contains Union, State and Concurrent Lists. Residuary legislative power belongs to Parliament under Article 248, read with Union List Entry 97.
Article 254 concerns repugnancy between Union and state laws on Concurrent List matters, including the important presidential-assent qualification.
Parliament may legislate on State List matters in specified circumstances, including Articles 249, 250, 252 and 253; learn the trigger for each.
Article 263 provides for an Inter-State Council; Article 262 concerns inter-state river-water disputes; Article 280 concerns the Finance Commission.

comparison: Consent of two or more states
confusion: The Inter-State Council and the Finance Commission are different bodies. River-water disputes have their own Article 262 framework.
recall: Who has residuary legislative power?
Parliament: Article 248 and Union List Entry 97.
Which Article allows Parliament to legislate after state consent?
Article 252, where two or more state legislatures pass the required resolutions.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The Inter-State Council and the Finance Commission are different bodies. River-water disputes have their own Article 262 framework.

title: Emergency Provisions
gist: Compare the three emergencies by trigger, approval period and effect.

points.html: Article 352: national emergency for war, external aggression or armed rebellion; parliamentary approval within one month, using the required special majority.
Article 356: failure of constitutional machinery in a state; approval within two months, followed by six-month periods subject to constitutional limits and safeguards.
Article 360: financial stability or credit threatened; approval within two months. Once approved, it continues until revoked, without six-month renewal requirements.

Article 358 concerns Article 19 during emergencies based on war or external aggression. Article 359 concerns a presidential order suspending the right to seek enforcement of specified rights, excluding Articles 20 and 21.

confusion: Armed rebellion can trigger Article 352, but it does not activate Article 358's special treatment of Article 19. Do not merge Articles 358 and 359.
recall: Which rights are protected against an Article 359 enforcement-suspension order?
Articles 20 and 21. The 44th Amendment safeguards are central to this distinction.
Which emergency needs approval within one month?
A national emergency under Article 352; the initial period for Articles 356 and 360 is two months.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Armed rebellion can trigger Article 352, but it does not activate Article 358's special treatment of Article 19. Do not merge Articles 358 and 359.
memory_hook: 352 / 356 / 360: national / state / finance. Initial approval: 1 / 2 / 2 months.

title: The Finance Commission
gist: The Finance Commission recommends how fiscal resources should be shared.

points.html: Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission constituted by the President every five years or earlier as considered necessary.
It consists of a chairman and four other members. Parliament determines qualifications and the manner of selection by law.
Its work includes distribution of divisible tax proceeds between Union and states, allocation among states, and principles governing grants-in-aid.
It also recommends measures to augment state Consolidated Funds to supplement local-body resources, based on State Finance Commission recommendations.

comparison: Policy institution; separate origin and role
confusion: Recommendations on sharing public resources are not the same thing as preparing the Union Budget or conducting a CAG audit.
recall: How many members make up a Finance Commission?
Five: one chairman and four other members.
Who constitutes it, and how often?
The President, every fifth year or earlier if considered necessary.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Recommendations on sharing public resources are not the same thing as preparing the Union Budget or conducting a CAG audit.

title: The Planning Commission/NITI Aayog
gist: Planning Commission and NITI Aayog are executive policy institutions with different approaches.

points.html: The Planning Commission was established by executive resolution on 15 March 1950; it was neither a constitutional nor a statutory body.
NITI Aayog was established on 1 January 2015 by executive resolution, replacing the Planning Commission.
The Prime Minister is Chairperson. The Governing Council brings state and Union Territory leadership into the policy forum.
NITI Aayog's emphasis includes cooperative federalism, policy advice and monitoring. Its role should not be confused with the Finance Commission's constitutional tax-sharing recommendations.

confusion: Replacing an institution does not mean its successor has every old power or funding role. Keep NITI's policy role separate from the old planning framework.
recall: Is NITI Aayog a constitutional body?
No. It was created through executive resolution, not directly by the Constitution.
What connects the two institutions at the top?
The Prime Minister chairs both the former Planning Commission and NITI Aayog.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Replacing an institution does not mean its successor has every old power or funding role. Keep NITI's policy role separate from the old planning framework.

title: Lokpal and Important Commissions
gist: Start with a body's legal basis, then learn appointment, tenure and function.

points.html: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 provides a statutory anti-corruption framework. Lokpal is not a body directly created by the Constitution.
The NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Its appointment and tenure provisions have been amended, so read historical questions by date.
UPSC and State Public Service Commissions are constitutional bodies under Articles 315 onward; Article 320 concerns their functions.
The Central Vigilance Commission is statutory. Different commissions may investigate, advise, recruit or recommend; sharing the word commission does not make their powers identical.

confusion: A commission's recommendation is not automatically a binding judicial judgment. Identify the powers actually given by its Constitution or Act.
recall: Which body here is created by Article 315?
The Public Service Commission framework, including UPSC and State PSCs.
Why are old NHRC eligibility questions date-sensitive?
The 1993 Act's provisions were amended; the current statutory position may differ from an old keyed answer.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A commission's recommendation is not automatically a binding judicial judgment. Identify the powers actually given by its Constitution or Act.

title: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions
gist: Special constitutional provisions for particular regions have distinct histories and purposes.

points.html: Part XXI contains temporary, transitional and special provisions. The heading does not make every provision identical in legal operation.
Article 370 concerned Jammu and Kashmir's former special arrangement. The 2019 constitutional and reorganisation measures changed that framework.
The book discusses the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh after the 2019 reorganisation; older questions still use the former state's institutions.
Articles 371 onward contain distinct provisions for particular states. Article 371A concerns Nagaland; Article 371J concerns the specified Karnataka region.

confusion: Do not apply a former Jammu and Kashmir state rule to the post-2019 Union Territory simply because an old PYQ uses the same place name.
recall: Which Part contains the provisions discussed here?
Part XXI: temporary, transitional and special provisions.
Are Article 370 and Article 371A interchangeable?
No. They concern different territories and different constitutional arrangements.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Do not apply a former Jammu and Kashmir state rule to the post-2019 Union Territory simply because an old PYQ uses the same place name.

title: Election Commission
gist: Separate who conducts elections from the legal rules governing each election.

points.html: Article 324 places supervision, direction and control of elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President with the Election Commission of India.
The Constitution provides for the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners as determined; appointments are made by the President, subject to parliamentary law.
Local-body elections are supervised by State Election Commissions, not the Election Commission of India.
Article 326 concerns adult suffrage. The 61st Amendment reduced the voting age from 21 to 18; registration, qualifications and disqualifications are governed by the electoral framework.

confusion: The CEC and other Election Commissioners do not have identical removal safeguards. Read Article 324(5) rather than assuming all members are removable in the same way.
recall: Who supervises Panchayat elections?
The State Election Commission under the local-government constitutional framework.
What did the 61st Amendment change?
The adult-suffrage age in Article 326, from 21 to 18.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The CEC and other Election Commissioners do not have identical removal safeguards. Read Article 324(5) rather than assuming all members are removable in the same way.

title: Political Parties
gist: Registration, recognition and legislative membership rules are three different topics.

points.html: Political-party registration is governed by the Representation of the People Act, 1951; recognition as a state or national party follows Election Commission rules.
The 52nd Amendment, 1985 added the Tenth Schedule on disqualification for defection. The 91st Amendment, 2003 altered this framework.
Voluntarily giving up party membership and voting or abstaining contrary to a binding party direction can engage the Tenth Schedule, subject to its provisions.
The merger exception has a two-thirds legislative-party threshold. The former one-third split exception was removed; old questions may refer to the earlier rule.

confusion: A party can be registered without being recognised as a national or state party. Party-status lists are snapshots, not permanent facts.
recall: Which amendment inserted the Tenth Schedule?
The 52nd Amendment, 1985.
What happened to the one-third split exception?
It was removed by the 91st Amendment; do not confuse it with the two-thirds merger provision.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
A party can be registered without being recognised as a national or state party. Party-status lists are snapshots, not permanent facts.

title: Constitutional Amendments
gist: An amendment question usually tests procedure, a landmark change or the basic-structure limit.

points.html: Some constitutional changes use an ordinary parliamentary majority outside Article 368. Article 368 amendments require the specified special majority in each House.
Certain federal provisions additionally require ratification by at least half the state legislatures. No joint sitting resolves an amendment-bill deadlock.
The 106th Amendment, 2023 concerns women's reservation in Lok Sabha and specified assemblies, with commencement/implementation conditions. The basic-structure doctrine constrains the amending power.

comparison: Special majority + at least half the states
confusion: Passing a reservation amendment and implementing reserved seats are different events. Article 334A contains the census-and-delimitation condition.
recall: Can a constitutional amendment bill be introduced in Rajya Sabha?
Yes. It can start in either House; both must pass it separately.
Which case is associated with the basic-structure doctrine?
Kesavananda Bharati, 1973. The doctrine limits the substance of constitutional amendments.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Passing a reservation amendment and implementing reserved seats are different events. Article 334A contains the census-and-delimitation condition.

title: Official Language
gist: Official language, scheduled language and medium of court proceedings are different classifications.

points.html: Article 343 specifies Hindi in Devanagari as the Union's official language and the international form of Indian numerals; legislation also governs continued use of English.
The Eighth Schedule has 22 languages in the book's constitutional snapshot. It began with 14; Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment, three languages by the 71st, and four by the 92nd.
Article 345 concerns state official languages; Article 348 concerns language in the Supreme Court, High Courts and authoritative legal texts, with qualifications.
Article 350A concerns primary-stage mother-tongue instruction for linguistic minority children; Article 350B provides for the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

confusion: The Constitution does not declare Hindi a national language. Eighth Schedule recognition also does not make every listed language a Union official language.
recall: How many languages were originally in the Eighth Schedule?
14. Later amendments raised the book's listed total to 22.
Which Article creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities?
Article 350B; distinguish it from the instructional safeguard in Article 350A.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The Constitution does not declare Hindi a national language. Eighth Schedule recognition also does not make every listed language a Union official language.

title: Panchayati Raj and Community Development
gist: Local self-government has three separate questions: representation, elections and finances.

points.html: The 73rd Amendment added Part IX and Schedule 11 for Panchayats; the 74th added Part IX-A and Schedule 12 for municipalities. Their commencement dates are 24 April and 1 June 1993 respectively.
Gram Sabha consists of persons registered in the village electoral rolls. The elected Gram Panchayat is a different institution.
Local-body terms are normally five years. State Election Commissions supervise elections; State Finance Commissions review the relevant local finances.

The constitutional minimum reservation for women is one-third, including the specified SC/ST seats; state legislation may provide a higher share. Panchayats and municipalities have different institutional structures.

confusion: One-third is the constitutional minimum for women's reservation, not a claim that every state's current law provides exactly one-third.
recall: How do Gram Sabha and Gram Panchayat differ?
Gram Sabha comprises the registered village electors; Gram Panchayat is the elected local body.
Who handles elections and who reviews finances?
The State Election Commission supervises elections; the State Finance Commission reviews local finances.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
One-third is the constitutional minimum for women's reservation, not a claim that every state's current law provides exactly one-third.
memory_hook: 73 village, 74 town; 29 village subjects, 18 town subjects.

title: Special Provision for Certain Classes
gist: Link representation, constitutional commissions and identification of protected classes without merging them.

points.html: Articles 330 and 332 concern SC/ST reserved seats in Lok Sabha and state assemblies; Articles 338, 338A and 338B concern the SC, ST and Backward Classes Commissions.
Articles 341 and 342 concern specification of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Article 340 concerns a commission to investigate backward-class conditions.
The 104th Amendment extended SC/ST seat reservation while Anglo-Indian nomination was not extended beyond the earlier seventy-year period.

The 106th Amendment inserted Articles 330A, 332A and 334A for women's representation and its implementation condition. The source's label 'Article 300 A' for Lok Sabha women's reservation is a printing error: read 330A.

confusion: The source's Article 300 A label in this chapter is wrong. Preserve awareness of the misprint, but learn the correct provision: 330A.
recall: Which Articles concern the SC and ST Commissions?
338 and 338A respectively; 338B concerns the Backward Classes Commission.
Does Article 300A reserve Lok Sabha seats for women?
No. It protects property. Women's Lok Sabha reservation is in Article 330A.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
The source's Article 300 A label in this chapter is wrong. Preserve awareness of the misprint, but learn the correct provision: 330A.

title: Miscellaneous
gist: This is a mixed chapter: organise international institutions and Indian public bodies separately.

points.html: The United Nations began on 24 October 1945. Its main organs have distinct deliberative, security, economic/social, judicial and administrative roles.
The Security Council has five permanent members; the General Assembly includes the UN membership. Do not transfer one body's voting rules to another.
The International Court of Justice is seated at The Hague. It is different from the International Criminal Court, despite their shared city.

The Indian portion includes accountability institutions, public administration and newer tools such as BHARATPOL, developed by the CBI for international police cooperation. Date-sensitive membership and office-holder questions need their original year.

confusion: Older UN-membership answers can become obsolete. Keep a historical question's answer separate from any later membership position.
recall: Which UN organ is seated at The Hague?
The International Court of Justice. The International Criminal Court is a separate institution.
Which Indian agency developed BHARATPOL?
The CBI, for facilitating international police cooperation; the book discusses its January 2025 launch.
Spot the trap: what distinction must you keep clear in this chapter?
Older UN-membership answers can become obsolete. Keep a historical question's answer separate from any later membership position.
